questions.title: What constitutes ‘similar’ services under the second DuPont factor when the parties’ services are not identical but are in the same financial services field?
questions.question_body: In this opinion the Board found the services of CC Serve (credit‑card services) and Apex (banking and financing services) to be ‘legally identical, in part’ and thus highly similar under DuPont factor 2. I’m having trouble understanding how the Court reconciles the fact that CC Serve doesn’t actually issue banks’ credit cards itself but instead partners with banks to manage the programs. Does the delegation of service to a bank change the analysis, or is the mere participation in the credit‑card offering enough to treat the services as the same? How does the Board justify the conclusion that the services ‘may emanate from a single source’?

questions.title: Why did the court vacate the Board’s finding on DuPont factor 6 while affirming the finding on factor 2?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that DuPont factor 6 requires consideration of similar marks for similar goods, but the Board limited the analysis to credit‑card services only, excluding other banking‑related services. Since the Court previously found the services to be 'highly similar' under factor 2, why does the Court now view the similarity requirement of factor 6 as ‘too narrow’? Aren’t the two factors supposed to be independent? What is the legal basis for the Court’s decision to require a broader universe of similar marks under factor 6?

questions.title: How does the Court apply the concept of commercial strength to a mark that has not been shown to be either ‘strong’ or ‘weak’?
questions.question_body: The Board concluded that CC Serve’s "ASPIRE" mark was ‘entitled to the normal scope of protection accorded inherently distinctive marks’ because it had not proved commercial strength, yet Apex had not shown weakness. The Court says this is legally flawed. Why is the lack of evidence for either strength or weakness insufficient for a decision on scope? What standard does the Court use when assessing the commercial strength of a mark?

questions.title: What is the role of ‘substantial evidence’ when the Board’s findings of fact on DuPont factors are contentious?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites M2 Software, Inc. v. M2 Commc’ns, Inc. to explain that findings of fact are reviewed for substantial evidence, while conclusions of law are reviewed de novo. In practice, how does this standard apply when the Board’s factual determination of, say, the similarity of services is challenged? Should we look for a 'reasonable mind' that could accept the evidence, or is there a different threshold when the findings directly influence the likelihood‑of‑confusion analysis?

questions.title: Why does the Court consider the ‘overall commercial impression’ of the marks under DuPont factor 1 to be affected by a reconsideration of factor 6?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that a different determination of the mark’s commercial strength or weakness from factor 6 may alter the ‘overall commercial impression,’ prompting the Court to vacate factor 1. What is the logical connection between the commercial strength of a mark and the overall commercial impression? Is there a precedent that directly links a change in factor 6 analysis to a change in factor 1 conclusions?

questions.title: Under what circumstances does the Board not need to consider all thirteen DuPont factors?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites that the Board 'need not consider every DuPont factor, only those that are relevant and of record.' In this case the Board considered factors 1, 2, and 6, but omitted several others. What criteria determine when a factor is deemed 'relevant and of record'? How does a party demonstrate that a particular factor must be considered?
